summary: Introductory walkthrough of Redwood's catalog navigation, compatibility matrix, and bench onramp. Focus on selecting open models for Verdant's customer-facing summarization product with cost/latency tradeoffs and ops constraints (VPC, KMS). Agreed next steps: share bench spreadsheet, run latency/cost sweep, schedule POC kickoff.
meeting_header: Date: 2027-04-06 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 minutes | Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE); Lena Torres (Verdant Head of Platform), Marcus Li (ML Engineer), Priya Rao (SRE), Noah Kim (Product)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Ethan and I from Redwood; Lena, Marcus, Priya and Noah from Verdant?
[00:07] Lena (Verdant): Yep that's right, thanks for fitting us in. We've got about 45 minutes — high level demo and then bench onramp discussion.
[00:15] Maya: Perfect. We're going to show the catalog UI flows in Console, how Optimize surfaces batching/quant recommendations, and then a short bench onramp path for open models. Ethan will jump into the compatibility matrix and perf tradeoffs.
[00:28] Ethan (Redwood SE): Quick note — I'll be toggling between the Console model view and the bench spreadsheet. Some of the model names might be slightly off in the auto captions, sorry in advance.
[00:35] Marcus: No worries. Two quick context points from our side: 1) we run a low-latency summarization endpoint for support tickets, target p95 < 300ms, and 2) we want to keep data in our VPC with KMS for keys.
[00:48] Priya: Also, cost is a factor — we want to estimate tokens-per-day and keep spend predictable; we may consider Dedicated if latency is hard to hit on hosted.
[00:58] Maya: Great context — fits exactly into the tradeoffs we'll walk through. Okay Ethan, take it away on catalog navigation.
[01:05] Ethan: Alright. I'm in the Redwood Console — top left is the Model Catalog. You can filter by architecture, seq length, and quantization compatibility. For Verdant's summarization use case I usually start by filtering for moderate context models (2k-4k) and then 'open' licenses.
[01:25] Lena: Quick Q — when you say 'open', do you mean permissive licenses only or also community models with non-commercial clauses?
[01:32] Ethan: The 'open' filter defaults to permissive (MIT, Apache) but you can expand to CC-like models. We also surface license caveats in the model card. Note: the detection isn't always perfect — sometimes the card will say 'license unknown' if upstream metadata is missing.
[01:45] Noah (Verdant): Is there a way to pin multiple model variants and route by latency? We have an edge case where short tickets need <150ms.
[01:54] Ethan: Yes — the routing policy supports multi-variant routes. You can set SLO targets and the smart router will prefer low-latency variants for short requests, fallback to higher-capacity models for long form. In Console it's under Deployments > Routing.
[02:06] Marcus: Can you show the compatibility matrix you mentioned?
[02:09] Ethan: Sure, opening the compatibility matrix for the shortlist. So here we have three candidate families: 'os-2k-lite', 'libra-3b', and 'tide-7b-quant'. The matrix shows hardware compatibility (A100, H100, Triton-style), quant profiles (int8, q4), kernel fit notes, and an estimated tokens/sec and median latency from Redwood's curated bench data.
[02:31] Maya: Important to call out — those bench numbers are representative for the sequence distributions we used. For Verdant we'll run a bench with your exact prompt set to get apples-to-apples.
[02:40] Priya: About the bench — what's the friction to run that with our data? We prefer to keep prompts sensitive, so files shouldn't leave our VPC.
[02:48] Ethan: We support two bench onramps: 1) you share redacted prompt samples and we run on hosted infra; or 2) we run the bench in your private deployment — Redwood Private — where the bench runner uses your VPC and never exfiltrates data. Option 2 requires a short setup with our ops team.
[03:02] Lena: We'll probably want option 2. Can you estimate setup time?
[03:06] Maya: Typically 3-5 business days for access and a bench run, depending on your infra approvals. We'll need an infra point of contact — Priya?
[03:12] Priya: Yep that works.
[03:14] Ethan: Back to the matrix — notice 'tide-7b-quant' has the lowest cost per token when using q4 profile, but the median latency is slightly higher on short requests because of kernel warmups for KV cache.
[03:26] Marcus: When you say KV cache warmup — that's the per-request prefix caching? We cache conversation history on our side.
[03:31] Ethan: Right — KV cache refers to the attention key/value cache. If you have many short requests with different prefixes, the benefit of caching is lower. Our Optimize recommendations will flag that and suggest smaller context windows or dedicated pool sizing.
[03:42] Noah: Curious if Optimize will recommend model-switching by route automatically or just batching/caching knobs?
[03:47] Maya: Optimize suggests batching, quant profiles, and model recommendations. For routing it's integrated — you can set cost vs latency tradeoff thresholds and Optimize will suggest a policy and which variants to include. You always get to review before applying.
[03:57] Lena: Can we see an example of the bench spreadsheet?
[04:00] Ethan: Opening the bench template — columns are: prompt_id, avg_input_len, avg_output_len, sample_tokens, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, cost_per_1k_tokens_est. We also have a column for 'compatibility notes' where kernel selection or memory pinch is flagged.
[04:18] Marcus: The cost estimates — how accurate are they for hosted vs dedicated?
[04:22] Ethan: Hosted estimates use our current host pricing; dedicated is shown as a per-GPU amortized cost plus throughput. For dedicated we show a recommended pool size to meet your SLOs and how that maps to monthly commit.
[04:33] Priya: Security — audit logs, key management, and retention. We require customer-managed KMS.
[04:38] Maya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and we log token-level traces to your retention window. We can also disable request logging on a per-route basis for PII-heavy flows.
[04:49] Lena: Any gotchas for open models that are finetuned downstream? License compatibility or redistribution?
[04:54] Ethan: Good call — if you fine-tune and redistribute, you must follow the upstream license. The catalog flags models where derivative restrictions apply, but legal should review for anything borderline.
[04:62] Speaker 6 (Auto): [inaudible]...
[05:08] Maya: Sorry, that was an awkward caption. Back to routing: a typical Verdant recommendation would be a 2-variant route: short requests -> os-2k-lite on low-latency dedicated pool; long requests -> tide-7b-quant on a cost-optimized pool with asynchronous fallback.
[05:24] Marcus: Sounds reasonable. For the bench run, what's a suggested sample size to hit statistically meaningful p95?
[05:29] Ethan: We recommend 500-1000 warm requests covering your traffic distribution. For p95 stability 1k is ideal.
[05:35] Noah: Do you support streaming outputs for partial responses? Our UX uses streaming to show incremental summary lines.
[05:41] Maya: Yes streaming is supported across hosted and private. There's also 'function call' style structured outputs if you want deterministic JSON responses.
[05:47] Marcus: Any mention of competitor differences? We looked at Anthropic for safety tools and OpenAI for throughput.
[05:53] Ethan: We often see Anthropic models having stronger instruction alignment but at different latency/cost points; OpenAI endpoints are optimized but less flexible for private deployments. Redwood's playbook focuses on picking the right open family and quant profile to approximate those tradeoffs while keeping deployment flexibility.
[06:08] Priya: Practical question — if we hit a sudden traffic spike, how does fallback work? Do you fail open to a cheaper model or queue requests?
[06:15] Maya: Our smart router supports both: you can configure to fallback to a higher-capacity, lower-cost variant or to enqueue with exponential backoff. We include metrics in Console so you can see how often fallbacks occurred.
[06:25] Lena: Let's talk POC scope — we want to validate p95 < 300ms for short flow, cost estimate for 1M tokens/day, and integration with our KMS. Is that feasible in a 2-week POC?
[06:36] Ethan: Yes — typical scope: week 1 setup + bench run; week 2 tuning + validation. We'll need prompt set, SLOs, and access for bench runner.
[06:44] Maya: I'll send the POC template after the call. Also sharing a bench workbook with prefilled candidate models so you can eyeball tradeoffs.
[06:51] Marcus: One more — how do rollouts work? Canary percentages?
[06:54] Ethan: We support canary by route, gradual ramp, and automatic rollback on regression signals tied to your eval suite. Console shows per-route performance and drift alerts.
[07:04] Noah: That rollback tied to evals is interesting — can we plug our own unit tests?
[07:08] Maya: Yes you can upload custom evals (prompt + expected) and Redwood will run them in the CI gating flow.
[07:14] Lena: Okay this has been really useful. Quick recap of next steps?
[07:18] Maya: Recap: 1) Maya share playbook deck + bench spreadsheet (Due 4/8). 2) Verdant provide 500-1k prompt samples and SLOs (Lena) by 4/9. 3) Ethan runs latency/cost sweep and shares results (Due 4/12). 4) Schedule POC kickoff 4/19 — Maya to send invite.
[07:36] Priya: Confirmed. Also we'll open a ticket for Private bench access with our security team.
[07:41] Marcus: Anything else on licensing? We'll loop legal if needed.
[07:44] Maya: Yep, legal review for any model with ambiguous license. We'll highlight which candidates to watch.
[07:50] Speaker 1 (Auto): Alright that's the end of transcription...
